pr_body:

#### What type of PR is this?

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug
/kind cleanup
/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
If `DoHTTPProbe()` returns an error as third return value, a probe worker treats it as a client failure and throws it away:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5973accf487eef985393cde200e7a4f9d09bc2e0/pkg/probe/http/http.go#L102-L108
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5973accf487eef985393cde200e7a4f9d09bc2e0/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L100-L111
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5973accf487eef985393cde200e7a4f9d09bc2e0/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L287-L291

When an error is raised while a prober is reading a response body, something is likely wrong with a server (container) such as hang up or abortion. This change returns `Failure` without an error in order to handle it as a server (container) failure in this case.

This PR also adds test cases for HTTP probe with failure modes such as disconnection, hang up and slow down, which are emulated by `agnhost liveness`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

-->
Fixes #122591

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

issue_context.title: Liveness probe with an error doesn't trigger container restart
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

We have a specific case when a health check would error out with `500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR`. In this particular scenario, the readiness probe will correctly mark pod unready but the liveness probe does not trigger a container restart.

Here are some more details:
1. Kubernetes Server Version: v1.24.16.
2. An application pod is running a single container.
3. Both readiness and liveness probes are `httpGet` and are hitting the same `/healthcheck` endpoint.
4. Healthcheck endpoint is responding with `500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR`.
5. The readiness probe does mark the container as "unready" as expected.
6. The liveness probe does not trigger a container restart, even after the multiple consecutive failures.

I confirmed that `restartPolicy: Always` and when I exec into the container and run curl, I do get the 500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR, the same as what I see in the application logs. As per documentation, a failing liveness probe should be triggering a restart but it is not happening.

Here's the log from kubelet:
```
Jan 03 17:34:20 ip-1-1-1-1 kubelet[5845]: E0103 17:34:20.352585    5845 prober.go:118] "Probe errored" err="unexpected EOF" probeType="Liveness" pod="mynamespace/application-abc
```

Also, looking at the code [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.24/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L115-L124) the error does seem to be captured correctly by the probe but restart is not initiated.

Somehow the error is not being handled gracefully I assume. If I change it to an invalid port and cause a timeout the container gets restarted as expected. Also, switching from `httpGet` to `exec` type of healthcheck and running `curl http://localhost:8000/healthcheck` does trigger a restart so I suspect there is some bug with the httpGet probe itself.

This is what I see in the events:
```
Liveness probe errored: unexpected EOF
Readiness probe errored: unexpected EOF
```

### What did you expect to happen?

A failing healthcheck in a liveness probe would trigger a container restart.

```
containerMessage="Container abc  failed liveness probe, will be restarted"
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a deployment with an app that is crashing and returns 500

Configure healthceck like so:
```
    livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        path: /healthcheck
        port: healthcheck
        scheme: HTTP
      initialDelaySeconds: 3
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 3
    name: abc
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
      name: healthcheck
      protocol: TCP
    readinessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        path: /healthcheck
        port: healthcheck
        scheme: HTTP
      initialDelaySeconds: 3
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 3
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

```console
$ kubectl version

```

I have the same problem on Kubernetes v1.28.7. A LivenessProbe receives an `HTTP/2 200` result and then the connection times out because there IS a problem with the container. Notwithstanding the 200 status, the probe result shows as: 

**Liveness probe errored: context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout or context cancellation while reading body)**

but the container really never gets restarted. I expect that it should be restarted if a liveness probe errored, shouldn't it?

/triage needs-information

We will need kubelet logs or repro steps to triage this issue further.

If a message is "Probe **errored**", no probe failure is reported because `err` is not `nil`:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4bb434501d9ee5edda6faf52a9d6d32a969ae183/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L103-L110

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4bb434501d9ee5edda6faf52a9d6d32a969ae183/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L287-L291

I'm not sure how to reproduce the error. However, I guess the error happened here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4bb434501d9ee5edda6faf52a9d6d32a969ae183/pkg/probe/http/http.go#L102-L108

We started to read a response body for just logging the cause of a failure at #8238. So, we can ignore a read error and judge a result based on only a status code. However, if a probe should fail in [the comment above](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/122591#issuecomment-1987686079)  where a connection error happened after the code 200 is received, it would be better to treat the read error as a probe failure like:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4bb434501d9ee5edda6faf52a9d6d32a969ae183/pkg/probe/http/http.go#L99

Original message:

Related to the OPs post, I think I'm encountering this same or very related bug, but with an exec liveness probe timeout. Notably different, in my case, the container remains in Ready state.
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3e88b6e1-3eb7-45cd-bf54-bf51d2dfdbc1)
              
To reproduce, a basic Deployment:
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: timeout-test
  labels:
    app: timeout-test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: timeout-test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: timeout-test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27.1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - sleep
            - "60"
          failureThreshold: 3
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          successThreshold: 1
          timeoutSeconds: 1
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 1
```

We're running v1.28.9-gke.1289002, and I confirmed that `ExecProbeTimeout` is enabled in our environment.
This is still an issue in `v1.26.15`

I hit this same issue with an http readiness probe:

```
          readinessProbe:
            failureThreshold: 2
            httpGet:
              path: /api/healthcheck
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 15
            timeoutSeconds: 5

  Type     Reason     Age                     From     Message
  ----     ------     ----                    ----     -------
  Warning  Unhealthy  54s (x1799 over 6h15m)  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
 ```

This is with Istio so that gets flipped over to go through Envoy, but the event is still the same. The 503 error for the readiness probe failed 1799 times. This is on EKS v1.29.10-eks-7f9249a.

Looking at this thread, in my experience if the readiness probe marks the pod as NotReady, then the livenessProbe does not actually lead to a restart. I wonder if the NotReady of the startUp probe and the NotReady of the readinessProbe are actually the same, but this would explain the behavior the OP mentioned.

It's also important to understand the difference between the 2 probes - an api healthcheck (in my opinion, of course and depending on the usecase too) should rarely be required for the readinessProbe, because you want the API to be be restarted if there's a problem, not stop getting traffic (which is what a readinessProbe failure would do).

The intent of the probes is actually clearly documented on https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/.

I'm sure everyone has read this, but just incase someone hasn't I thought I'd share this.
